Count violations for several rules at once

Source: R/tally_violations.R
tally_violations.Rd

Evaluates a set of named rules and returns one row per rule with the number of violating rows. Where a chain of expect_none() calls stops at the first abort, tally_violations() evaluates every rule, so a delivery with five problems is reported as five problems in one go.

Usage

tally_violations(data, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble.

...

Rules that describe a violating row. Name them; an unnamed rule is named after its expression.

Value

A tibble with one row per rule and the columns rule (name), n (number of violating rows) and rows (list of their row numbers in data, for data[rows[[i]], ]).

Details

Why "tally"

To tally is to keep count, as with tally marks or dplyr::tally(). The name marks the difference from the expect_*() family: those judge (a check passes, warns or aborts), while tally_violations() only counts and never warns or stops. Severity stays a separate, explicit decision, made afterwards by piping the tally into expect_empty(). The same tally therefore serves both as a hard gate in production and as a report you read or send on.

The result is itself a violation set once filtered, which closes the loop back to expect_empty():

df |>
  tally_violations(
    "Missing id"       = is.na(id),
    "Negative amount"  = amount < 0,
    "Unknown industry" = !branche %in% codebook$branche
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(n > 0) |>
  expect_empty(abort_msg = "The delivery failed validation")

Kept unfiltered, it is a validation report: send it back to whoever made the data, e.g. with write_excel() after dropping the rows column.

Rules follow dplyr::filter() semantics: each must give TRUE for a violating row, and NA counts as no violation. Rules are evaluated with dplyr::mutate(), so if_any(), across() and grouped data work.

See also

expect_empty(), expect_none()

Examples

tally_violations(ggplot2::mpg,
  "Few cylinders"  = cyl < 4,
  "High mileage"   = hwy > 40,
  "Missing model"  = is.na(model)
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   rule              n rows     
#>   <chr>         <int> <list>   
#> 1 Few cylinders     0 <int [0]>
#> 2 High mileage      3 <int [3]>
#> 3 Missing model     0 <int [0]>
